items.name: watch_cancel
items.description: Cancel a watch and its queued callback deliveries. An already in-flight delivery may still arrive.

items.name: watch_create
items.description: Watch a web page and report when it changes. Give url and kind. kind=content_changed: the page text changed. kind=text_appeared: one of terms shows up (works with url, or with query to watch search results). kind=price_below: the product price falls under price (needs price and currency). kind=price_dropped: the price falls below the last one seen (needs currency, no price). The first check is silent. Read changes with watch_events, or give webhook_url to receive them.

input.name: currency
input.description: Three-letter currency code such as EUR. Required for price_below and price_dropped.

input.name: expires_in_seconds
input.description: The watch stops after this many seconds.

input.name: idempotency_key
input.description: Reuse for a retry of exactly the same operation/input.

input.name: interval_seconds
input.description: Seconds between checks.

input.name: kind
input.description: What counts as a change.

input.name: max_checks
input.description: The watch stops after this many checks.

input.name: max_pages
input.description: Pages read per check of a query watch.

input.name: max_units
input.description: Usage budget for the whole watch.

input.name: notify_initial
input.description: Also report the first observation.

input.name: price
input.description: Price limit. Required for kind=price_below, not allowed otherwise.

input.name: query
input.description: Web search to watch instead of a page. Only with kind=text_appeared.

input.name: terms
input.description: 1 to 5 words or phrases to wait for. Required for kind=text_appeared, not allowed otherwise.

input.name: url
input.description: Public http or https page to watch. Give url or query, not both.

input.name: webhook_url
input.description: Optional https address that receives signed change events.

items.name: watch_events
items.description: Read detected changes, supporting evidence and delivery status for a watch in the current scope.

input.name: after

items.name: airfield_get
items.description: Get comprehensive information for one airfield or airport by ICAO code. Sections include core data and ratings, landing and parking fees with fuel prices, contact details, community pilot reports (PIREPs), car-rental availability, and webcam discovery. Always read the PIREPs carefully — they contain first-hand local knowledge from pilots who flew there: transport links, facilities, restaurants, hotels, fuel quirks, and operational tips not found in structured data. Provide arrival/departure and optionally tailsign for live Aerops fee and app2drive car-rental pricing. ground_ops.landing_fees.li

input.name: arrival
input.description: Planned arrival time, supplied together with departure for live Aerops landing-fee and app2drive car-rental pricing. Include a timezone; times are normalized to UTC.

input.name: departure
input.description: Planned departure time, supplied together with arrival for live Aerops landing-fee and app2drive car-rental pricing. Include a timezone; times are normalized to UTC.

input.name: icao
input.description: Airfield ICAO code, such as EDAZ, from airfield_search items.icao or search results.id.

input.name: pireps_limit
input.description: Number of recent community pilot reports to include when the pireps section is requested.

input.name: sections
input.description: Detail sections to retrieve for this airfield. Omit to retrieve all sections; each returned section includes its availability status.

input.name: tailsign
input.description: Aircraft registration used for aircraft-specific Aerops landing fees, including the country prefix (e.g. D-EABC). Must be registered with Aerops.

items.name: airfield_list_by_h3
items.description: Get map or route-planning markers for batches of H3 cells. Returns lightweight airfield markers with runway, rating, fuel, and weather-availability signals so clients can filter and rank candidates efficiently.

input.name: fuel_types
input.description: Fuel filter tokens: 100LL, JET-A, MOGAS, UL91, UL94, or G100UL. Matches any selected fuel. These are filter tokens, not numeric taxonomy fuel IDs.

input.name: h3_cells
input.description: H3 cells at resolution 3 covering the area to search. Use h3_cell values from airfield_get or airfield_search, or compute cells with an H3 library. Supply hexadecimal cell strings, using a 0x prefix if the value contains only digits.

input.name: ifr_only
input.description: Set true to include only airfields marked as supporting instrument flight rules operations.

input.name: min_rating
input.description: Minimum average community pilot-report rating for matching airfields.

input.name: min_runway_length
input.description: Minimum length in meters of the longest runway at the airfield, regardless of surface.

input.name: other
input.description: Required border-entry services or special-entry eligibility. Multiple selections are combined with AND semantics.

input.name: paved_only
input.description: Set true to include only airfields with a paved runway.

input.name: result_limit
input.description: Maximum number of markers to return across all supplied cells. Check truncated and total_count to detect omitted matches.

items.name: airfield_search
items.description: Search airfields by ICAO, airport name, city, or place name, or browse a scoped region by continent, country, and state. Returns compact operational summaries by default or richer section payloads per result; place names fall back to nearby-airfield geo search, while batch mode defers live pricing to per-airfield lookups.

input.name: arrival
input.description: UTC ISO8601 arrival or ETA. Enables live Aerops landing-fee pricing and live app2drive car-rental pricing.

input.name: continent
input.description: Continent value from taxonomy_list(kind: continents). For region browsing, supply together with country_code and state instead of query.

input.name: country_code
input.description: Country code from taxonomy_list(kind: countries) items.code, such as DE, for the region to browse.

input.name: cursor
input.description: Opaque data.next_cursor from the previous region-search response. Reuse with the same region filters to retrieve the next page; query mode does not use cursors.

input.name: departure
input.description: UTC ISO8601 departure or ETD. Enables live Aerops landing-fee pricing and live app2drive car-rental pricing.

input.name: limit
input.description: Number of airfields requested for this query or region page. Query mode caps the requested count at 20.

input.name: pireps_limit
input.description: Number of recent community pilot reports to include per airfield when the pireps section is requested.

items.description: Screens a shortlist of up to 15 candidate names in one call: the trademarks on file near each name, the companies registered under it, and whether its domains are registered. Ranks them fewest conflicts first: by how close the nearest mark is, then by companies registered under the name and domains taken, then by how many near marks there are. No account needed. Optional `classes` (Nice class numbers) make marks filed only in unrelated classes weigh less; without them, a mark in any class counts. The Swiss company register and the .ch and .com domains are always checked; `countries` ("UK", "SG

items.name: dismiss_conflict
items.description: Clear one hit as not-a-threat. Reversible — it moves to the Cleared list. Takes `jurisdiction` and `app_no` exactly as they appear on a conflict in the user's conflict list. A cleared hit, such as an unrelated business or the user's own filing, stops being surfaced.

items.name: filer_activity
items.description: What the filers this user follows have filed lately. Studio and up.

items.name: filing_landscape
items.description: Filing activity in a Nice class — volume by month and the busiest filers. Signed-in. Answers "how crowded is my space" and "who keeps filing near me". Pass a Nice class (9, 42, 36…), optionally an office code ('EM', 'US', 'GB', 'CH'), and a window in months. EVERY COUNT IS OF OUR MIRROR, NOT OF THE OFFICE, and the two differ by a lot for some offices right now. Each office carries its own `coverage`, and any office whose mirror is behind is named in `do_not_quote`: for those offices a low count means filings not yet ingested, not filings that were never made.

items.name: follow_filer
items.description: Follow an adversary — every filing they make, anywhere. Studio and up. Different from watching a name: this catches what they do NEXT, which is usually a different name in a class the user doesn't hold.

items.name: get_credit_balance
items.description: How many credits this user can spend and what each paid tool costs, in credits. Free to call. `remaining` is what can be spent now: `monthly_left` (included with their plan, resets each month) plus `topup_balance` (bought, never expires). `prices` is credits per call, by tool.

items.name: holder_read
items.description: Who a holder is and how they file — the read on an adversary. Free. Computed from their whole register book: how much of it they let lapse, whether their marks cluster where they trade or spray across unrelated classes, and the leverage that gives counsel. Returns the evidence behind each finding; it draws no legal conclusions about the holder. Corporate identity from PermID comes with `attribution`, its CC BY 4.0 credit.

items.name: my_conflicts

items.name: my_deadlines
items.description: Renewals and closing opposition windows for this user. Each deadline has a `kind`: `opposition` carries a real date; `window_pending` means a filing is still in examination and nothing is running yet; `window_unknown` means a live threat whose deadline cannot be dated; `window_closed` means opposition is gone and the route is cancellation.

items.name: my_watches
items.description: The names this user is watching.

items.name: opposition_window
items.description: How long you have to oppose a filing in a given trademark office, and from when. Twenty registers, each with the provision the window comes from. The trap this answers: most offices run opposition BEFORE registration, from publication of the application, but a minority — Switzerland, Germany, Japan, Sweden — register the mark first and run the window from publication of the REGISTRATION. Applying one office's rule to another invents a deadline that never existed. Accepts a country name, an office name or a two-letter code ('japan', 'JP', 'EU').

items.name: run_investigation
items.description: Research a trademark holder on the open web and return a cited dossier: who they really are (an operating company, a shell, a known squatter), their notable trademark activity or disputes, and any red flags. Signed-in. Spends one credit — included credits first, then purchased ones. A failed run costs nothing, and calling again for the same holder within 30 minutes returns that dossier at no charge (`reused: true`). The dossier is AI-written from cited web sources: research to check, not register fact.

items.name: screen_mark
items.description: Screens one brand name against trademark registers. No account needed. Returns the registered and pending marks closest to the name (up to 25), each with a similarity tier, and the registers those marks are filed in. EU marks come from EUIPO's search; the other registers are read from Antevo's copy, refreshed from each office, so a filing from the last few days can be missing. It is a screen, not clearance.

items.name: suggest_classes
items.description: Which Nice classes a business like this files in. No account needed, and no register is searched: it maps the description onto the Nice classification. The question people cannot answer for themselves: not "is my name taken" but "taken in WHAT". Nice has 45 classes and the numbering is opaque — software you download is class 9, software you log into is class 42, and selling other people's goods is class 35 whatever the goods are. Filing in one and not the other is the most expensive routine mistake in the process. Takes a description of the business and returns the classes similar businesses f

items.name: check_ollama_loopback

Given the diagnostic output your own machine (or AI tool) already produced locally - this tool never reaches your machine or network, it only reasons over what you send it. Resolves to PASS, FAIL, or UNVERIFIABLE (never guessed). On FAIL, returns the complete fix. Nothing you submit is stored, logged, or retained.

items.name: disable_alert_relay
items.description: Ends this API key's ArrowMem Guard alert relay enrolment. No arguments. Your family link stops resolving, your old topic gets one fixed notice that the relay ended, and every relay attribute is removed from your key's row; it mints nothing, and calling it again is a no-op. Your key, usage, cap and subscription are untouched; call enrol_alert_relay afterward to enrol again. Paid tool - requires a valid API key. Spends one call.

Mints a relay token stored beside your key and returns an alert topic derived from it (subscribe to it once, in a push notification app, on your own phone), plus a one-time family link you share with the one person you want able to check on you if a call sounds like you and asks for money. No arguments. On an already-enrolled key it returns the SAME topic and no new family link (never re-shown once given). To replace the topic or the link use rotate_alert_relay; to end the enrolmen

Reads the page's byline, the addresses the page publishes, and Hunter.io; when no author is found it returns the site's contact address and contact page instead. Every email comes with its source. Costs 0.1 credits when an author is found (billed in whole credits every 10 lookups); free otherwise. Overwrites the saved author fields. Obtain user confirmation before running it over many pages.

input.name: url
input.description: Cited page URL, e.g. "example.com/blog/best-tools". A contact already saved under this exact URL (for example one the Outreach page saved for a query variant its URL rules list separately) is used first. Otherwise protocol, "www." and the query string (tracking parameters) are ignored, as on the Outreach page. The page is always read at the URL given.

items.name: get_ai_insight
items.description: Read one stored AI insight in full, by its id from get_ai_insights: its title, headline, body, suggested action, why it happened (with reasons and their pages), its numbers (facts, each with the table it came from), its move (subject, metric, current and previous values, the direction that is good news, and a definition of what the series counts and what it is out of), its evidence (topics, competitors, prompts, URLs), and the scope its numbers were computed under (window, comparison period, Default schedule, the prompts active at the analysis, prompt-type filter, the models the citation table

input.name: insight_id
input.description: The insight's id, from get_ai_insights.

items.name: get_ai_insights
items.description: List the website's stored AI insights: the precomputed cards on the AI Insights page, each a verified finding of one past analysis, newest analysis first and higher impact first. Each has its id, title, headline, category, impact, the days its numbers cover (window), the time the analysis ran (analyzed_at), its status (available, done, or discarded = hidden by the team), the team's rating, and its move's subject and metric. Call this first for an open-ended request for insights or for what to do ('give me some insights', 'what's interesting', 'what should I prioritize'), and answer from these

input.name: offset
input.description: How many to skip: the previous read's next_offset.

input.name: status
input.description: The lifecycle to list: available (default), done, or discarded (hidden by the team).

items.name: get_ai_search_value
items.description: AI Search Value for a website: topic-market value, captured value range, headroom, coverage, value-weighted AI share of voice, per-topic detail, and modeled attributed contribution.

items.name: get_attribute_metrics
items.description: Get cumulative brand trait (attribute) metrics: for each brand-perception keyword (e.g. 'Affordable', 'Slow Support'), how many AI responses mentioned it across the date range, and the percentage. `positive` selects the observation direction and defaults to true when omitted. `total_responses` is the denominator: responses in the date range that mention the brand AND had attribute extraction run on them. It is NOT every response for the website — responses that never mention the brand are excluded, and Athena samples which responses get extraction, so un-analyzed ones are excluded too. Compute

items.name: get_attribute_observations
items.description: Get individual brand trait (attribute) observations: each row is one AI response describing one entity (the brand or a competitor) with one brand trait, including the response excerpt as `text_span`. `score` runs from -1 to 1 and its sign always matches `positive`; its magnitude (0.1 to 1.0) is how strongly the wording praises or criticizes. `score` is null when the observation was not scored (extracted before scoring existed, or no valid value was recorded); for direction only, use `score ?? (positive ? 1 : -1)`. Omit `positive` for both directions. `sort: "intensity"` (the default) returns t

input.name: attribute_ids
input.description: Attribute UUIDs to filter to (from get_attributes), as an array even for one id. Omit for every active attribute.

input.name: entity_ids
input.description: Entity UUIDs to filter to, as an array even for one id: the website_id for the brand itself, competitor ids from get_competitors for competitors. Omit for every entity.

input.name: page_num
input.description: Zero-indexed page number. Defaults to 0.

input.name: page_size
input.description: Rows per page, 1 to 100. Defaults to 40.

input.name: positive
input.description: true for favorable observations only, false for critical ones only. Omit for both directions.

input.name: sort
input.description: "intensity" (default): strongest first, unscored last, then newest. "recent": newest first.

items.name: get_attribute_time_series
items.description: Get the daily trend for ONE brand trait (attribute), brand and competitors side by side — how mentions of a keyword like 'Affordable' moved over time. Requires an attribute_id: call get_attributes first to discover ids. `positive` selects the observation direction and defaults to true when omitted. Days with no data are returned as zeros, so the series is gap-free and chartable. Denominators are per-side, not the day's whole response set: brand_percentage divides by that day's responses that mention the brand (and had attribute extraction run), and competitor_percentage by responses that menti

items.name: get_attributes
items.description: List the brand traits (called attributes in the API) tracked for a website: brand-perception keywords such as 'Affordable' or 'Slow Support'. Athena extracts these from AI model responses. Brand traits are direction-neutral; `positive` selects the directional series and defaults to true when omitted. Use this to discover attribute ids, then get_attribute_metrics for how often each is mentioned, or get_attribute_time_series for one attribute's trend over time.

items.name: get_brand_facts
items.description: List a website's brand facts from the Knowledge Base, newest first, with offset paging. By default excludes facts generated by Oracle analysis; pass include_oracle=true to include them. Filters: pillar, review status (default approved), source type, and unfiled=true for facts not under any published pillar (unfiled and pillar_id are mutually exclusive).

items.name: get_brand_kit
items.description: Read a brand kit as the Brand Profile editor shows it, to inspect or change it: the draft name, the eight guidance fields as text (voice is the writing direction), voice settings (1-5 or auto), tone traits, the kit's writing rules with ids, and the website's global writing rules with ids, plus draft and published versions. Omit kit_id for the website's default kit; available_kits lists every kit. Content generation uses a kit's published version, so has_unpublished_changes means the draft differs from it. Guidance fields longer than the clip come back shortened and listed in truncated_fields;

input.name: fields
input.description: Guidance fields to return whole (up to 12,000 characters) instead of clipped at 4,000. Needed before a find edit on a clipped field.

input.name: kit_id
input.description: The brand kit to read. Omit it for the website's default kit; available_kits lists every kit.

items.name: get_citation_rate_cumulative
items.description: Get cumulative citation rate — average citation rate for each competitor across the date range. citation_rate is absolute (share of all responses); relative_citation_rate is the share of responses citing the website or any tracked competitor.

items.name: get_citation_rate_time_series
items.description: Get citation rate over time — how often AI models cite (link to) the website, grouped by day. citation_rate is absolute (share of that day's responses); relative_citation_rate is the share of that day's responses citing the website or any tracked competitor.

items.name: get_competitor_attribute_metrics
items.description: Get brand trait (attribute) metrics per tracked competitor: for each competitor and each brand-perception keyword (e.g. 'Affordable'), how many AI responses mentioned that keyword for that competitor, and the percentage. Use with get_attribute_metrics to compare the brand against competitors. `total_responses` is per-competitor: responses in the date range that mention THAT competitor and had attribute extraction run on them. Each competitor therefore has its own denominator, and none of them is the website's total response count. `positive` selects the observation direction and defaults to tr

items.name: get_competitors
items.description: List competitors tracked for a website

items.name: get_content_citation_prompts
items.description: For a single tracked content item, list every prompt whose AI responses cited it — with citations, citation %, and estimated impressions. Use after get_tracked_content to drill into which prompts a given URL is appearing for. This is CITED-BY, measured over the requested date range, not the targeting the page was written for: an empty prompts array means no AI response cited this URL in that window, which is expected for new or never-cited pages and is not missing data. For the prompts a page was written to target, read `prompts` on get_content_detail (or prompt_ids on list_content) — those co

items.name: get_content_detail
items.description: Fetch the full detail of a single tracked content item — its brief and body text (drafts, optimize rewrites, snipes, authored and scraped pages), plus status, cited source URLs, and links. Use after get_tracked_content to read the actual text behind a content_id. A status of generated_brief means the brief is ready while the article is still being written. Pages registered via track_content_urls return a null body and null status until their page text is fetched from the app — a null body on an external page means not fetched yet, not missing content; citation tracking does not need the body.

items.name: get_content_draft
items.description: Read the current draft text of a content item — the article body as it stands right now, including every revision applied so far. Use this before revise_content to see what you are changing, and after it to confirm the result. A status of generated_brief means the brief is ready while the article is still being written, so body may still be empty. For the full record (cited urls, links, social posts) use get_content_detail instead.

items.name: get_content_hub_sheets
items.description: List the Content Hub tabs/sheets configured for a website. Use to discover available tabs (e.g. 1st-party content, 3rd-party placements, Reddit) before calling get_tracked_content with a specific sheet_id (metrics; excludes in-flight pipeline items) or list_content (every item including unpublished drafts).

items.name: get_content_status
items.description: Get the normalized pipeline status (running | succeeded | failed) for one content row, plus the raw stage behind it. Read-only. Poll once per contentId returned by create_content (content.pipeline.start). A stage of generated_brief with status running means the brief is ready and waiting — for a non-auto-approve draft it stays there until approve_brief is called, so do not treat running as always in progress. Not meaningful for tracked pages (track_content_urls / external rows): they have no generation pipeline and report running with a null stage forever — read them via get_tracked_content or

items.name: get_content_version
items.description: Read the full text of one saved version of a content item. Use it to compare two passes (fetch both and diff them yourself) or to check what an earlier version said before restoring it.

items.name: get_content_versions
items.description: List the saved versions of a content item, newest first. Each entry carries its version number, label, how it was produced, and who made it. Use it to see how a draft evolved, then get_content_version to read a specific one, or restore_content_version to go back to it.

items.name: get_available_products
items.description: Returns the canonical Autodesk product catalog (closed set). Each item has: product_name, product_code, and release_codes. Use this to discover or validate product values for other product-scoped tools. Not required if valid product context is already available. Terminology: release_codes = the code only (e.g. 2025), not the human-readable release name (release_name, e.g. 'AutoCAD 2025').

items.name: search_help_content
items.description: Search Autodesk Help/Support documentation and return the most relevant documents for a user question. Use when: - The user asks how to do something in an Autodesk product. - The user reports an error (include the exact error text/code in the query). - The user needs official troubleshooting steps or reference documentation. Call shape (recommended): - Always pass: `query`, `locale`. - If your agent has a default product context, pass it directly via `product_code` (preferred) or `product_name`. - Pass `release_code` only when you can validate it for that product. Behavior: 1) Locale: - Read `

input.name: locale
input.description: Required. Locale used to scope search/results (language/region). Use the locale from context (do not guess).

input.name: max_results
input.description: Optional. Maximum number of results to return. Default is 5. Maximum allowed is 50.

input.name: product_code
input.description: Optional. Product code filter (preferred). First check your context for product_code, then call `get_available_products` to validate/normalize it. Use only the exact product_code returned by `get_available_products` (do not guess). If provided with product_name, both must refer to the same product.

input.name: product_name
input.description: Optional. Product name filter. First check your context for a product name, then call `get_available_products` to validate/normalize it. Use only the exact `product_name` returned by `get_available_products` (do not guess). Prefer product_code if available; if both product_code and product_name are provided, they must match.

input.name: query
input.description: Required. Keyword-rich search text. Include product + task/feature, and exact error codes/messages when relevant. Use the user's wording when possible. Write the query in the same language as `locale`. Maximum 1500 characters. Do not include secrets, credentials, or personal data.

input.name: release_code
input.description: Optional. Product-specific release identifier (often looks like a year, but may be alphanumeric/variant). First check your context for a release, then call `get_available_products` to validate/normalize it. Only pass an exact `release_code` returned for the resolved product (product_code/product_name). If you cannot validate it, omit release_code rather than guessing.

input.name: sources
input.description: Restrict which sources to search. Defaults to all sources on this deployment when omitted. sfdc_articles: support/knowledge-base articles. product_documentation: official product documentation. aps_api_documentation: APS API documentation. Choose based on the user question.

input.name: address

input.name: chain_id

input.name: session_id

items.name: get_block_info
items.description: Get block information like timestamp, gas used, burnt fees, transaction count etc. Can optionally include the list of transaction hashes contained in the block. Transaction hashes are omitted by default; request them only when you truly need them, because on high-traffic chains the list may exhaust the context.

input.name: chain_id
input.description: The ID of the blockchain

input.name: include_transactions

input.name: number_or_hash

input.name: session_id

items.name: get_block_number
items.description: Retrieves the block number and timestamp for a specific date/time or the latest block. Use when you need a block height for a specific point in time (e.g., "block at 2024-01-01") or the current chain tip. If `datetime` is provided, finds the block immediately preceding that time. If omitted, returns the latest indexed block.

input.name: chain_id
input.description: The ID of the blockchain

input.name: datetime
input.description: The date and time (ISO 8601 format, e.g. 2025-05-22T23:00:00.00Z) to find the block for. If omitted, returns the latest block.

input.name: session_id

items.name: get_chains_list
items.description: Get supported blockchain chains with their chain IDs. Ethereum Mainnet is `chain_id` `1`; use this tool to resolve any other chain. Use this when another tool needs a supported `chain_id` and only the chain name, ecosystem, or native currency is known. Prefer a narrow `query` to avoid returning the full registry to the agent. Do not rely on partial numeric chain ID queries such as `1`, because matching is substring-based and may return many chains.

input.name: query
input.description: Optional case-insensitive substring filter applied to chain name, chain ID, native currency, and ecosystem. Prefer narrow text terms over partial numeric chain IDs because matching is substring-based.

input.name: session_id
input.description: Opaque session identifier.

Example: To check the USDT balance of an address on Ethereum Mainnet, you would use the following arguments: { "tool_name": "read_contract", "params": { "chain_id": "1", "address": "0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7", "abi": { "constant": true, "inputs": [{"name": "_owner", "type": "address"}], "name": "balanceOf", "outputs": [{"name": "balance", "type": "uint256"}], "payable": false, "stateMutabili

items.name: run_session

items.name: execute_analytics_query
items.description: Answer a natural-language question about an enterprise organization's learning analytics (enrollments, completions, active learners, skills, program usage). Routes the question through the Enterprise Analytics control plane, which resolves it to governed metrics and returns structured results (KPIs, tables, and optional charts). Use for aggregate reporting questions scoped to the caller's organization — not for catalog/course search.

input.name: includeCharts
input.description: Whether the response should include chart/visualization specs alongside raw results. Defaults to true. Set false when the caller only needs the underlying numbers.

input.name: includeComparison
input.description: Whether to include period-over-period comparison / benchmarking in the response. Defaults to false. Set true only when the question implies a comparison ("vs last quarter", "trend", "change over time").

input.name: organizationId
input.description: Third-party organization id to scope the query to. Leave unset if you administer a single organization (it is auto-detected). If you administer multiple, call list_enterprise_organizations first, ask the user which one, then pass that organizationId here. Ignored on the header/per-client-scoped path.

input.name: query
input.description: A natural-language enterprise-analytics question, phrased the way an admin would ask it. The control plane classifies intent, resolves metrics against its catalog, generates SQL, and executes it against the analytics warehouse. Keep named entities (program names, skills, date ranges) verbatim. Examples: "show total enrollments by program", "how many learners completed a course last quarter", "active users in the Data Science program this month". Max 500 characters.

items.name: get_course_material
items.description: Returns the full ordered curriculum for one Coursera course: modules, lessons, and item titles. Requires a courseId returned by search_courses. Do not call it without one. Use when the learner has a specific course in hand and asks what it covers, how it is structured, how long a module runs, or where a topic appears in the sequence. Returns structure and titles only. It does not return lecture content, transcripts, or teach the material. If the learner wants to learn the material rather than inspect the outline, use learning_canvas.

input.name: locale
input.description: BCP 47 locale code inferred from the language the user wrote their prompt in (e.g., 'en-US', 'fr-FR', 'de-DE', 'ja-JP', 'pt-BR', 'ko', 'zh-CN'). Base this on the user's prompt text, not their UI language setting.

items.name: list_enterprise_organizations
items.description: List the enterprise organizations the current user administers (id + name). Use this to let the user pick an organization before calling execute_analytics_query — specifically when they administer more than one organization and haven't said which one. If they administer exactly one, execute_analytics_query resolves it automatically and you do not need this tool.

items.name: search_courses
items.description: Returns a ranked list of Coursera courses matching a topic, with title, provider, rating, duration, level, and enrollment link. Use when the learner wants to see or choose content: find, browse, compare, or get a link to courses on a subject, or asks what Coursera offers on X. Returns catalog data only. It does not teach, explain, or run a practice session. If the learner wants to build the skill in this conversation rather than pick something to enroll in later, use learning_canvas instead.

input.name: courseSearchQuery
input.description: Generate a simple query to use to search for courses, something that a user would input into the search bar on Coursera. Include the subject and, if possible, the difficulty level (e.g., Beginner Python, Advanced Marketing Analytics).

input.name: desiredDuration
input.description: How long the learner wants the course to be. Allowed values: UNDER_SIXTY_MINUTES, LESS_THAN_TWO_HOURS, ONE_TO_FOUR_WEEKS, ONE_TO_THREE_MONTHS, THREE_TO_SIX_MONTHS, SIX_TO_TWELVE_MONTHS, ONE_TO_FOUR_YEARS. Set only when the learner explicitly mentions a time commitment (e.g., "I have a weekend", "want a multi-month program"). Leave unset when unconstrained — any other value fails validation and the filter is dropped.

input.name: locale

items.name: deepstack_counter
items.description: Use when the user states a thesis or a claim about the AI economy and wants the strongest case against it. Returns the side the claim sits on (or the question, when no side label fits), the strongest case against that side from a voice outside it, dated and linked, more opposing voices, and the dated tests that settle it; below the relevance floor, that DeepStack has no formed side on the claim.

input.name: claim
input.description: The thesis as the user states it, for example “AI demand is real”.

input.name: limit
input.description: How many further opposing voices to return after the strongest case.

items.name: deepstack_docket
items.description: Use when the user asks what will decide a dispute, what to watch, or the next dated test. Returns the dated tests that will settle each story, from today forward: date and precision, status, the event, the resolver (which series, release or earnings print decides it) and the story, each with its URL.

input.name: include_past
input.description: Also list tests dated before today.

input.name: include_signal
input.description: Also list the tests that have no date and resolve on a signal.

input.name: part
input.description: Only the tests of one part.

input.name: window_days
input.description: How far ahead to look.

items.name: deepstack_entity
items.description: Use when the user asks what the voices argued about a company, or what a person argued, in The Buildout; by slug, ticker or name. Returns where it appears, the figures the stories reported, each argument attributed, dated and linked, and for a listed company the delayed market snapshot with its source. Never a score or a ranking.

input.name: kind
input.description: Narrow the lookup to companies, to people or to the organizations that contribute argument (listed with the people).

input.name: name
input.description: The name, when the slug is not known.

input.name: slug
input.description: The entity slug, as in [REDACTED URI]<slug>/ or /people/<slug>/.

input.name: ticker
input.description: A listed company’s ticker, for example NVDA.

items.name: deepstack_results
items.description: Use when the user asks what resolved and how the Call fared. Returns the tests that came in: verdict, what happened with the primary source and the number, what it did to the Call, and the rule that no hit rate is shown until ten results exist.

items.name: deepstack_search
items.description: Use when the user asks where informed investors disagree on a topic of the AI economy, or wants DeepStack’s published analysis on a company, a person or a question; returns the matching stories, sides, tests and entities with their canonical URLs, or answers “DeepStack has no formed side on …” with up to three nearest items, labeled as nearest. Use it first when the slug or name is not known.

input.name: kinds
input.description: Restrict the hits to these kinds; all kinds by default.

input.name: limit
input.description: How many hits to return.

input.name: query
input.description: Words to look for: a company, a person, a theme, a figure.

items.name: deepstack_sides
items.description: Use when the user asks for the bull and bear case, who disagrees with a thesis, the counter-argument, or what would change a side’s mind. Returns, for one story by slug or part number, The DeepStack Call and its side, every attributed, paraphrased voice on each side with its date and source link, the strongest case against each side, where voices cross, and the dated tests that settle it.

input.name: part
input.description: The part number, as an alternative to the slug.

input.name: slug
input.description: The story slug.

items.name: deepstack_story
items.description: Use when the user wants one Part of The Buildout read in full, by slug or part number: headline, dek, The DeepStack Call (stance, conviction, three actions, what would change the call, the side it takes and the case against it, the next dated test), key numbers, the full text as plain paragraphs, the dated tests, any result, the companies and people named, and the sources, each with its URL.

input.name: detail
input.description: “summary” leaves out the body paragraphs.

input.name: part
input.description: The part number in The Buildout, as an alternative to the slug.

input.name: slug
input.description: The story slug, as in [REDACTED URI]<slug>/.

A cautious signal doesn't by itself mean bad law: a court with authority over the case declined to follow it or limited it (declined to extend its rule to a new situation, leaving the rule intact), or a court without that authority rejected it and no court with authority has followed it. A later court distinguishing the case on its facts does

items.name: find_cases_that_cite

Returned citing cases include case_id when a Descrybe case is identified.

A note that later history for this case may be missing is a coverage limitation for some courts and dates, not a negative signal about the case.

input.name: case_id
input.description: Descrybe canonical case identifier, formatted like c1514149, rd68382347 or so2500012520251110, returned as case_id by Descrybe case search, case-text search, case-reference lookup, or citation-extraction results. input.name: case_id
input.description: Descrybe canonical case identifier, formatted like c1514149, rd68382347 or so2500012520251110, returned as case_id by Descrybe case search, case-text search, case-reference lookup, or citation-extraction results. Not a reporter citation, docket number, opinion ID, CourtListener ID, or other third-party identifier.

Each result includes case_id, the Descrybe canonical identifier accepted by known-case tools.

items.description: Semantic/concept search over U.S. non-case primary law, including statutes, regulations, constitutional provisions, court rules, session laws (enacted bills, and federal public laws), and the Federal Register from 1995: final rules, proposed rules, agency notices, and executive orders and other presidential documents (doc_type all leaves out proposed rules and notices unless one is cited, as in 89 FR 12345 or EO 14110), and federal agency guidance (official guidance, not law: manuals such as the MPEP, guidance documents, IRS notices and revenue procedures) and agency rulings and opinion letter

Build the three-record hardening pack that makes a NON-SENDING domain unusable for spoofing: a Null MX, a hard-fail SPF record, and a p=reject; np=reject DMARC record. For parked, redirect and brand-defensive domains only — NEVER for a domain that sends any mail, including transactional or one legacy system. Ask the domain's owner whether it sends any email BEFORE calling, then call with the bare domain (e.g. example.com) and confirm_no_mail: true only if they said it sends none — a call without it is a

input.name: confirm_no_mail
input.description: Send true only after the HUMAN who owns the domain has told you it sends no email at all; false or omitted is always refused, so ask them first instead of calling. Never set it on your own judgment or because a scan looked quiet. It unlocks the question only; the server independently re-checks DNS for evidence of mail and refuses when it finds any.

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain to check, e.g. example.com. Bare registrable names and subdomains both work; scheme, path or port do not belong here. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

input.name: rua_email
input.description: Mailbox to receive DMARC aggregate (RUA) reports, as a plain address like dmarc@example.com. Strongly recommended: without it nobody can see who sends as the domain.

items.name: check_bimi
items.description: Use this when the user asks how to get their logo shown in Gmail, Yahoo, Apple Mail or other inboxes (BIMI), whether their BIMI setup works, or why their logo does not show. A live read of one host's BIMI setup: the DMARC gate (BIMI needs p=quarantine or p=reject; dmarc_sources names each policy read and why it does or does not count), the published default._bimi record, the logo (fetched and checked as SVG Tiny PS) and any certificate (certificate.trust_verified is true for a mark certificate for this host, in date, chaining to a Mark Verifying Authority root, false with trust_reason when not

input.name: certificate_url
input.description: Optional https:// URL of the VMC or CMC certificate (PEM) for the candidate logo, added to the record as a=. Only used together with logo_url.

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain to check, e.g. example.com. Bare registrable names and subdomains both work; scheme, path or port do not belong here. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

input.name: logo_url
input.description: Optional https:// URL of a candidate SVG logo (port 443, no spaces, ; or ,). When given, that logo is checked instead of the published one and generated carries the BIMI record for it. Omit it to check what the domain already publishes.

items.name: check_dkim_selector
items.description: Use this when the user asks whether DKIM is set up for a sending platform, whether a specific selector exists, or why DKIM fails. Check ONE specific DKIM selector on a domain — the exact selector the sending platform uses (e.g. `google`, `s1`), which a full scan's common-selector sweep may miss. Returns the verdict, its explanation, and the published key record when one resolves. No fix record is returned: a DKIM key is generated by the sending platform, so the fix is always to publish what that platform gives the owner.

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain to check, e.g. example.com. Bare registrable names and subdomains both work; scheme, path or port do not belong here. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

input.name: selector
input.description: The DKIM selector to probe — the name before ._domainkey, e.g. 'google', 'selector1', or a dotted form like 's1.prod'. The sending platform's settings page names it; it is not guessable from the domain.

items.name: check_domain_names
items.description: Use this when the user is choosing a domain name and wants to know which candidates are already registered. Pass up to 20 candidate names in ONE call (never one call per name). Each name is read live from its registry over RDAP: status is registered | not_registered | unknown. registered carries the registry's own status words (registry_status) and expires_at when published; being_deleted: true (pendingDelete / redemptionPeriod) means it is still registered and cannot be registered yet. not_registered means the registry holds no registration for the name: relay it as exactly that, never as 'av

input.name: names
input.description: 1 to 20 candidate domain names to check in ONE call, e.g. ["brightlane.com", "brightlane.io"]. Registrable names only (example.com, example.co.uk), not subdomains; duplicates are checked once. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

items.name: check_domain_verification
items.description: Use this only for DNS Doctor's own ownership TXT challenge on a domain the user already added to their DNS Doctor account (add_monitored_domain). For a TXT record another service asked for (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Shopify or any site verification), use check_record instead. Check whether the ownership TXT record for a domain the user has added is visible yet, and mark it verified when it is. The result says WHICH outcome occurred and which nameservers were asked, so you can tell 'not published yet' from 'published with the wrong value' from 'our lookup did not complete' — a lookup tha

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain, e.g. example.com. For add_monitored_domain: any registrable domain the linked account owns (re-adding one it already monitors returns that row). For check_domain_verification and get_domain_records: a domain this account already monitors, verified or still pending. Any other name — another account's, or one nobody monitors — is refused as not found; ownership is never disclosed.

items.name: check_lookalikes
items.description: Use this when the user asks about lookalike, look-alike, typosquat or impersonation domains of their domain, or whether someone has registered a name close to theirs. DNS-only: checks the closest variants of the name and returns facts — how many resolve and how many accept mail, with up to ten resolving names (each with the kind of variant, whether it accepts mail, and same_infra when it points at the domain's own nameservers or mail servers, which usually means the owner registered it defensively). Never a verdict: relay the names as facts and never call one malicious — resolving only means t

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain to check, e.g. example.com. Bare registrable names and subdomains both work; scheme, path or port do not belong here. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

items.name: check_propagation
items.description: Use this when the user asks whether a DNS change has propagated globally, or why a record shows in one place and not another. Check whether a DNS change has propagated GLOBALLY: six vantage points (five owner-run probes across four continents plus this server's own resolver) each read the same name through several resolvers, and the grid plus a deterministic verdict comes back. Call it after the human publishes a record — you have ONE network vantage point, and a record that resolves for you can still be missing elsewhere. `name` is the exact name (www. is not stripped, _dmarc.example.com work

input.name: expected_value
input.description: Optional value the record should now hold, e.g. '1.2.3.4' or the new DMARC record text. Supply it and each cell is reported as match or mismatch against it; omit it and the check only reports whether the vantage points agree with each other.

input.name: name
input.description: The exact DNS name to look up, e.g. example.com, www.example.com or _dmarc.example.com. It is used as given — a leading www. is NOT stripped and underscore labels are kept — so pass the name the record is actually published at, not the registrable domain.

input.name: record_type
input.description: The record type to read at that exact name (default A). SPF and DMARC records are TXT — pass TXT with the right name rather than expecting a derived query name.

items.name: check_record
items.description: Use this when the user asks whether a DNS change has landed, wants a DNS record looked up, or wants to verify a record they just published — or whenever answering needs the live value of a record. Reads the record from the domain's OWN nameservers (cache-free) and from two public caching resolvers. `kind` is one of spf|dmarc|txt|mx|cname|a|aaaa — pass the kind, not a query name: `dmarc` reads TXT at _dmarc.<domain> and `spf` reads apex TXT, each filtered to the matching record. `host` prepends a label (txt, cname, a and aaaa only). When the user names the domain but not the host, check the dom

input.name: domain
input.description: The domain to check, e.g. example.com. Bare registrable names and subdomains both work; scheme, path or port do not belong here. Unicode names are accepted and normalized to punycode.

input.name: expected_value
input.description: Optional: the exact value just published (e.g. the DMARC record text, a verification token, '10 mx.example.com'). Given it, the verdict tests for that value and an 'edit' also checks the names a misplaced edit usually lands on (found_at).

input.name: host
input.description: Optional label to prepend to the domain (e.g. 'mail' to check mail.<domain>) — honored for txt, cname, a and aaaa only; spf, dmarc and mx derive their own query name.

input.name: kind
input.description: Which record to read; the right query is derived from it — 'dmarc' reads TXT at _dmarc.<domain> filtered to v=DMARC1, 'spf' reads the apex TXT filtered to v=spf1, so don't prefix the domain yourself.

items.name: check_reverse_dns
items.description: Use this when the user asks about reverse DNS, PTR records, or FCrDNS for a mail server IP. Check one sending IP's forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS): reads the IP's PTR record, then resolves that hostname back and reports whether it returns to the same IP. `verdict` is confirmed (the pair agrees — what receivers want to see), ptr_missing (the IP publishes no reverse record), or mismatch (a PTR that does not resolve back). A PTR on its own proves nothing, because the IP's operator writes its own reverse zone — only the forward confirmation is evidence, so never report a bare PTR as verifie

input.name: ip
input.description: The sending IP to check, IPv4 or IPv6. Must be a public address — private, loopback and CGNAT ranges have no meaningful reverse DNS and are refused.

items.name: count_spf_lookups
items.description: Use this when the user asks about SPF 'too many lookups', the 10-lookup limit, an SPF PermError, or whether an SPF record is valid. Validate an SPF record and count what it costs. Returns `record_valid` (the record parses as RFC 7208 SPF), `findings` (per-term diagnostics), `has_pass_all` (a `+all` that authorizes the whole internet to send as this domain), `multiple_all` (more than one `all`, which makes everything after the first unreachable), the parsed `terms`, and the lookup count against the limit of 10 with `over_limit`/`near_limit` and the `offending_mechanisms` that push it over. Pass

input.name: domain
input.description: A bare domain like example.com whose PUBLISHED SPF record should be resolved and counted recursively (nested includes cost lookups too). Send exactly one of domain or record, never both.

input.name: record
input.description: The full SPF record text starting with v=spf1, e.g. 'v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all' — never a domain name. Counts this record's own terms only. Send exactly one of domain or record, never both.

items.name: generate_dmarc_record
items.description: Use this when the user asks to create, generate or write a DMARC record for a domain that has none. Build a DMARC record from scratch for a domain that has none, using a validating engine — never compose one yourself. `policy` is none|quarantine|reject; optional `rua_email` (aggregate-report destination), `subdomain_policy`, and `strict_alignment`. Every generated record carries np=reject — the DMARCbis tag for non-existent subdomains, which can have no legitimate aligned mail — independently of the p= you choose. The generated record is re-validated before it is returned. Present it verbatim;

input.name: policy
input.description: The requested p= policy: 'none' monitors only, 'quarantine' sends failing mail to spam, 'reject' refuses it outright. Start at 'none' unless the domain's aggregate reports already justify enforcement.

input.name: rua_email
input.description: Mailbox to receive DMARC aggregate (RUA) reports, as a plain address like dmarc@example.com. Strongly recommended: without it nobody can see who sends as the domain.

input.name: strict_alignment
input.description: Set true to emit strict alignment (aspf=s adkim=s), requiring an exact domain match instead of the organizational-domain match. Leave false unless you know every sender aligns strictly.

input.name: subdomain_policy
input.description: Optional sp= policy for subdomains when it should differ from the main p= policy. Omit to let subdomains inherit p=.

items.description: Use this when a signed-in operator asks what changed on a monitored domain, whether its website went down, or what the monitoring has flagged. Read the monitoring alert log for the domains the caller's account monitors, newest first, including website uptime incidents (site_down, site_partial, site_recovered, and site_blocked when the site's protection refuses our checks). Needs a connected DNS Doctor account or an API token. Each row carries id, domain, type, check, summary, a deterministic detail map, created_at, email_sent_at, acknowledged_at and delivery_class — a 'dashboard_only' row was

input.name: domain
input.description: Optional filter to ONE of the account's verified monitored domains. Omit it for every domain the account monitors; an unowned or unknown name is refused as not found.

input.description: Page size, 1..100 (default 50). Page down with `before` before you advance `since`, or you will skip every row you did not receive.

input.name: since
input.description: Optional ISO-8601 timestamp: return alerts created at or after it (INCLUSIVE). Poll by storing the newest created_at you have seen and passing it back — rows repeat rather than go missing, so de-duplicate on id.

input.name: type
input.description: Optional alert-type filter, e.g. 'record_changed'. An unknown value is rejected rather than silently returning an empty page — omit it unless you know the exact type.

items.name: get_domain_records
items.description: Read the records a domain the user monitors still needs: the ownership check while it is unverified, and once verified the DMARC reporting record plus whether we have OBSERVED that record published. Read-only: it issues nothing — if a verified domain comes back with no reporting record yet, call check_domain_verification once, which issues it. Print every record host and value EXACTLY as returned — never rewrite, reformat or improve a record string. items.name: create_cluster
items.description: Creates an AlloyDB cluster. ***Requirements*** * The project the cluster is being created in must exist. * The location the cluster is being created in must be a supported AlloyDB location. ***Usage*** 1. Call `create_cluster` to create a cluster. 2. This will return a long-running operation that indicates the progress of the cluster creation. 3. You can poll the status of the operation using the `get_operation` tool. 4. Once the long-running operation is complete, the cluster will be in a READY state.

input.name: clusterId
input.description: Required. The cluster ID is the unique user-assigned ID of the cluster. It should be an alphanumeric string that can can consist of lowercase letters, numerical digits, or dash ("-") characters. This field is REQUIRED.

input.description: Optional. The Express configuration for the cluster, which lets you create an AlloyDB Express cluster instead of a standard AlloyDB cluster. If unspecified, a standard AlloyDB cluster is created.

input.description: The network is the VPC network that the cluster will reside in. Specifying this field will enable Private Google Access. This field is OPTIONAL, and if specified, it should have format like "projects/{project}/global/networks/{network_id}". This field should not be be specified if psc_enabled is true.

input.name: parent
input.description: Required. Identifier. The parent resource in which to create the cluster. The value must have a format of projects/{project}/locations/{location}. - {project} is the project that the cluster resides in. This field can be specified either as: - Project ID: An alphanumeric string that can consist of lowercase letters, numerical digits, or dash ("-") characters. - Project number: A valid base-10 encoded positive integer. - {location} is the Google Cloud region that the cluster resides in. Regions will have format like "us-central1" or "us-west2". The field is REQUIRED.

input.name: pscEnabled
input.description: Configures whether Private Service Connect is enabled for the cluster. This field is OPTIONAL. If neither network nor psc_enabled is specified, the default behavior will be to enable Private Service Connect.

This field can be specified either as: - Project ID: An alphanumeric string that can consist of lowercase letters, numerical digits, or dash ("-") characters. - Project number: A valid base-10 encoded positive integer. - {location} is the Google Cloud region that the cluster resides in. Regions will have format like "us-central1" or "us-west2". - {cluster_id} is the ID of

input.name: pscInstanceConfig
input.description: Optional. The configuration for Private Service Connect (PSC) for the instance. If automatic creation of PSC endpoints is desired, then configs for PSC auto connections must be specified. If unspecified, PSC endpoints will need to be created manually. This field is OPTIONAL.

input.description: Optional. Enables a publicly available Domain Name System (DNS) domain name at which the AlloyDB instance can be reached. Public DNS is only supported for instances in AlloyDB Express clusters, where it enables public access to the instance instead of `enable_public_ip`. This field is OPTIONAL. You can have multiple read pool instances per cluster, but they can only be created after the primary instance has been created. This field is OPTIONAL. If unspecified, it will default to PRIMARY.

Pass as_of with the encounter's date of service to also check the code was in effect on that date — ICD-10 sets change every October 1 and sometimes mid-year, and a code not in effect on the date of service is not billable (current set: FY2027). Codes retired from the current set are reported as retired, with the period they were in effect.

input.name: contentFormat
input.description: Optional media format filter. Must be exactly 'AUDIO' or 'VIDEO' (case-sensitive). Set this only when the user explicitly asks for audio content or video content. This is separate from contentType: contentType chooses guided/talks/music, while contentFormat chooses AUDIO/VIDEO. - 'AUDIO': audio-first content - 'VIDEO': video content Omit this parameter when the user does not state a format preference. input.name: contentLangs

input.description: Filter by content type. Must be exactly 'guided', 'talks', or 'music' (case-sensitive). - 'guided': Teacher-led meditation practices (body scans, breathwork, visualizations, mindfulness exercises, sleep meditations etc) - 'talks': Teachings, dharma talks, lectures on meditation, spirituality, philosophy, psychology, and wellbeing topics - 'music': Instrumental tracks with no voice (sleep music, ambient, nature sounds, binaural beats, focus music, relaxation music) Omit this parameter to search across all three content types. INTENT HEURISTICS (IMPORTANT): - If the user asks to learn/understand

input.name: lengthRange
input.description: Filter by content duration in minutes. Format: 'AtoB' where A and B are positive integers. Examples: - '5to15' finds 5-1

When used, keep all other parameters identical to the previous request and set 'page' to the 'nextPage' value returned by the prior response. Omit this field (or treat as page 1) for any new or modified search. This is an internal continuation mechanism, not a user-facing option — the user asks for "more", they don't pick a page number.

input.description: Natural language search for meditation and wellbeing-themed content. QUERY RULES (IMPORTANT): - Keep queries broad unless the user explicitly asked for something narrow. - Prefer 1–3 core keywords (topic/tradition/practice) over long phrases. - Use the user's language as-is for the initial search. Do NOT translate to English. - If the user explicitly requests a language, translate the query into that language for the first call (e.g., "sleep meditation in Spanish" -> query: "dormir"). - Do NOT add extra techniques (e.g., "breathwork", "body scan", "somatic") unless the user asked for them or t

IMPORTANT: Do NOT apply this filter when publisherName is provided or the user requests a specific teacher/publisher. Use when user specifies gender preference ("female voice", "male teacher") or omit to show all voices.

WHEN TO USE: - Finding providers by name (e.g., 'Find Dr. John Smith') - Finding providers by specialty (e.g., 'Cardiologists in Boston') - Finding organizations (e.g., 'Mayo Clinic locations') - Verifying clinical trial investigators have US credentials - Building provider networks by location or specialty - Finding all providers at a specific facility USE npi_lookup INSTEAD FOR: - When you already have a specific NPI number - Getting full details including raw API response SEARCH REQUIREMENT

input.name: address_purpose
input.description: Which address to search: LOCATION=any practice location, MAILING=mailing address, PRIMARY=primary practice location, SECONDARY=secondary practice locations. Default searches both mailing and practice addresses.

input.name: city
input.description: City name. For military addresses use 'APO' or 'FPO'. Special chars allowed: & ' : , / - ( ) . # " ;

input.name: country_code
input.description: Two-letter country code. 'US' for United States. Can be sole criterion only for non-US countries.

input.name: enumeration_type
input.description: Filter by provider type: 'NPI-1' = Individual providers (physicians, nurses, etc.), 'NPI-2' = Organizations (hospitals, clinics, etc.). Cannot be sole search criterion.

input.name: first_name
input.description: Provider first name (Individual NPI-1 only). Supports trailing wildcard with min 2 chars (e.g., 'Jo*'). Special chars allowed: & ' : , / - ( ) . # " ;

input.name: last_name
input.description: Provider last name (Individual NPI-1 only). Supports trailing wildcard with min 2 chars (e.g., 'Smi*'). Special chars allowed: & ' : , / - ( ) . # " ;

input.name: limit
input.description: Results per request. Default: 10, Maximum: 200. Use with skip for pagination.

input.name: number
input.description: 10-digit NPI number. Rarely used in search - use npi_lookup for direct NPI queries.

input.name: organization_name
input.description: Organization name (Organizational NPI-2 only). Searches Legal Business Name, DBA, Former LBN, Other Names. Trailing wildcard supported (min 2 chars). Special chars allowed: & ' @ : , / - ( ) . # " ;

input.name: postal_code
input.description: 5 or 9 digit ZIP code. 5-digit codes match all 9-digit variants. Trailing wildcard supported (e.g., '212*' for all NYC ZIPs starting with 212).

input.name: skip
input.description: Number of records to skip for pagination. Maximum: 1000. Combined with limit, allows accessing up to 1,200 total results.

input.name: state
input.description: Two-letter US state abbreviation (e.g., 'CA', 'NY', 'TX'). Cannot be sole search criterion - must include another parameter.

input.name: taxonomy_description
input.description: Provider specialty or taxonomy description. E.g., 'Internal Medicine', 'Cardiology', 'Oncology', 'Family Practice'. Wildcard supported (min 2 chars).

input.name: use_first_name_alias
input.description: Expand first name to include common aliases/nicknames. Default: true. E.g., Robert also finds Bob, Rob, Bobby. Set false for exact match only.

Format: Exactly 10 digits, numeric characters only (0-9) 2. items.name: web_fetch
items.description: Purpose: Fetch and extract relevant content from specific web URLs. Use only when web_search excerpts are insufficient for the task at hand. Ideal Use Cases: - The user asked about a specific URL or page - You need exact wording or quotes that excerpts may have truncated - You need full-page analysis (long article, document, or page structure) - web_search excerpts are conflicting or clearly insufficient to answer For multiple independent extraction objectives, make separate web_fetch calls concurrently. Put related URLs that share one objective in a single call.

input.name: allow_live_fetch
input.description: Whether live fetching is allowed. Leave true for the freshest available content. Set false to use cached content only, which makes web_fetch much faster by avoiding the source website, but may return older content.

input.name: full_content
input.description: Prefer leaving this off. The default excerpt mode returns LLM-optimized snippets focused on your objective — they are much smaller, cheaper, and usually all you need. Only set to true when you explicitly need the entire page as markdown (e.g. reading a long article in full, or running a document through a downstream summarizer). Warning: enabling full content can return a large amount of content — often tens of thousands of tokens for a long article. This may exceed your MCP client's tool-output limit and will substantially increase response size and latency.

input.name: model_name
input.description: The identifier of the LLM model making this tool call (e.g. 'claude-opus-4.7', 'gpt-5.5', 'gemini-2.5-pro'). Before the first call, verify the exact active model slug from trusted runtime/session metadata or active client configuration. Pass the full slug verbatim; never shorten or substitute a model-family alias like 'gpt-5'. Used for product analytics only; does not affect search behavior.

input.name: objective
input.description: Natural-language description of what information you're looking for from the URLs. Limit to 200 characters.

input.name: search_queries
input.description: Optional keyword search queries (3-6 words each) used together with objective to focus excerpts on the most relevant content. Pass the queries from the prior web_search call that surfaced these URLs, if applicable.

input.name: session_id
input.description: Stable identifier for the current conversation. Generate a random value (UUID or 32+ character hex string) at the start of your session and reuse the exact same value on every web_search / web_fetch call. Do NOT change it between turns. Used for free-tier rate limiting and correlating your tool calls in our logs; ignored on paid-tier keys.

input.name: urls
input.description: List of URLs to extract content from. Must be valid HTTP/HTTPS URLs. Up to 20 URLs per request.

items.name: web_search
items.description: Purpose: Perform web searches and return LLM-friendly results, including excerpts that are usually sufficient to answer directly without a follow-up fetch. Ideal Use Cases: - Answering questions that require fresh or current information - Research, comparison, documentation, and troubleshooting questions - Broad tasks where multiple `search_queries` can be issued in a single call For multiple independent objectives, make one web_search call per objective concurrently. Put related query variations for the same objective in a single call's search_queries list.

input.name: model_name
input.description: The identifier of the LLM model making this tool call (e.g. 'claude-opus-4.7', 'gpt-5.5', 'gemini-2.5-pro'). Before the first call, verify the exact active model slug from trusted runtime/session metadata or active client configuration. Pass the full slug verbatim; never shorten or substitute a model-family alias like 'gpt-5'. Used for product analytics only; does not affect search behavior.

input.name: objective
input.description: Natural-language description of what the web search is trying to find. Try to make the search objective atomic, looking for a specific piece of information. May include guidance about preferred sources or freshness.

input.name: search_queries
input.description: Concise keyword search queries, 3-6 words each. They may use site: with a bare domain (such as site:example.com), but never a URL path after the domain and never quoted phrases. At least one query is required; provide 2-3 for best results. For broad tasks, you can include multiple related queries in a single call instead of chaining web_search calls. The queries should be related to the objective.

input.name: session_id
input.description: Stable identifier for the current conversation. Generate a random value (UUID or 32+ character hex string) at the start of your session and reuse the exact same value on every web_search / web_fetch call. Do NOT change it between turns. Used for free-tier rate limiting and correlating your tool calls in our logs; ignored on paid-tier keys.

Examples: "Is RSV worse in CT than NY?", "Compare diabetes in Texas vs California", "Do wastewater and ED visits agree on COVID?"
